findings: config/production.env sets CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=0, which unconditionally overrides base.env's 300 via the `{...base, ...override}` spread in loadConfig, so production silently runs with caching disabled while docs/base config claim 300s

The disabling value was introduced as a one-off debug change ('debug: temporarily disable cache to reproduce issue #412') directly in production.env, the file actually loaded for the production environment, rather than in a scoped/temporary override, dev config, or via a runtime flag
The debug CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=0 change was never reverted after issue #412 was resolved — it has persisted undetected in production for eight months

The debug cache change was bundled into the same commit as an unrelated, intentional DB_POOL_SIZE=50 change, violating single-purpose/atomic commit practice; this makes the diff harder to review, makes `git revert` impossible without also undoing the legitimate pool-size change, and likely let the debug line slip past reviewers who were focused on the pool-size change

There is no comment, TODO, expiry marker, or tracking ticket reference in production.env next to CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=0 indicating it is temporary/debug-only, so nothing distinguishes it from an intentional permanent setting

loadConfig performs a blind shallow-merge of override onto base with zero validation — there is no schema/sanity check (e.g., rejecting or warning on CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=0 or other semantically dangerous values) before the merged config is used
There is no config-drift or config-vs-documentation check (test, CI assertion, or startup validation) that would catch production values silently diverging from the documented/expected 300-second TTL
No monitoring/alerting exists (or none is mentioned) on cache hit rate or effective TTL that would have surfaced caching being completely ineffective in production over an eight-month period

The override-file design itself is inherently risky: any key present in an environment-specific file silently and completely overrides the base value with no diff/audit log of what production.env changes relative to base.env, making exactly this kind of silent, long-lived override easy to introduce and hard to detect
